#7662. Ignition, Inc.: MSP Mac Help Desk Guru (work from home)

Ignition is one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and the only fractional IT firm that specializes in the venture-backed technology ecosystem.

Fully Remote · Work from home · Full-time (Eastern or Pacific time zones) · Apple-first

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

⠀ You'll be the front line: helping with what you can, researching what you can't, and pinging the rest of the team when you're genuinely stuck. That last part is a skill, not a weakness — knowing when to ask is half the job.

We're one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and one of the only certified Apple Premier Partners — that’s kinda like getting knighted by the ghost of Steve Jobs. We started where you’d expect to find Macs (creative agencies, non-profits, education) but our primary clients today are cutting-edge, venture-backed AI SaaS startups, VC and private equity firms, registered investment advisors — many of them operating under stringent compliance expectations (SOC 2, SEC). That means we hold ourselves to a higher standard than the scrappy shop we started as. Polished, reliable, security-minded work is the baseline now — but always with a smile!

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We teach each other what we know, cover for each other when life throws a punch, and care a little too much about doing things the right way. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

We move fast, priorities shift, it’s not always documented (whatever it is), our tool set and list of supported platforms is sprawling, and some days the to-do list is longer than you'd like. If you can stay warm under pressure, create order out of chaos, learn new stuff fast because you love it, and speak up when you need help, you'll thrive here.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. As they say, the price of freedom is eternal vigilance.

The tech you'll work with (and grow into)

Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

Yes, PCs too — about one-third of our users are driving Windows

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 admin consoles

Identity and access — SSO, MFA, and security keys (Okta, Entra ID, Yubikey, and friends)

Lots of other security tools — our stack is constantly evolving and may vary from client to client

The everyday productivity stack — Slack, Zoom, conference-room AV, networking basics (Meraki), and endpoint tooling

⠀ You don't need to know all of this. You need to be the kind of person who wants to. As you grow, there's a clear path into infrastructure administration, project architecture and implementation, and — for the right person — security and compliance work (phishing simulations, endpoint detection, SOC 2 / CIS / SEC readiness, due diligence questionnaire support, etc.). That's where our most senior people live, and it's wide open.

The hard requirements — we won't move forward unless you:

Can work standard business hours in Eastern or Pacific time zones (we currently need both)

Have a quiet home workspace and reliable broadband

Have proven Apple aptitude — you actually use and like the Apple ecosystem

Have at least 5 years of IT support experience on the job.

⠀ Everything else — and this is the longer list, on purpose. We figure technical skills are teachable; character takes a lot longer. So we're looking for someone who:

Genuinely cares — about clients, teammates, and doing right by people

Loves to learn, and proves it in how they spend their time

Reads, and writes clearly — clear writing is clear thinking, and you'll do a lot of it

Stays calm and kind with a frustrated person on the other end of the line

Can tell the difference between good customer service and fantastic customer service, and refuses to settle for the former

Notices when something's being done inefficiently and fixes it (you may boast about it later, that’s fine)

Proofreads their own work (yes, we noticed whether you proofread your application)

Has a sense of humor, and doesn't take themselves too seriously

Our company founder/CEO is headquartered in the Bay Area. We work with innovative, ambitious companies developing AI products. Our team members hold a range of opinions about whether AI is “good or bad” for humans, but at the end of the day, we embrace the plain fact that it is here, we must embrace it to evolve, and our clients increasingly depend on us to help them embrace it, too, to help them evolve and stay competitive.

Our CEO's opinion: AI will not replace human labor any time soon; rather, AI is a new opportunity to either (a) get things done faster, or (b) get a much higher quality of output than before. If you’re an AI tinkerer, great! We want to hear how you’re using it and see your latest vibe project. If you’re allergic to AI or have no interest in learning new habits to work effectively with it, this is not the place for you.

Base salary: Applicants outside the USA will be compensated according to your local employment market. For applicants closer to the junior side who are located in the USA, $50,000–$65,000/yr, depending on experience level and your local geographical price index. With experience, comp goes up from there. Genuinely experienced, more senior candidates can be slotted higher — let's talk.

Type & location: Full-time, work from home, fully remote. Eastern or Pacific time zones.

Benefits: Medical / dental / vision for the employee, 401(k) with employer contribution, 2 weeks of PTO annually to start, and a stipend for your home internet.

The first step is really easy and only takes 10 minutes — no resume, no cover letter, no essays. Here's how:

Take this online Culture Index assessment (about 10 minutes): We use it to screen for people whose natural wiring fits how our team works.

If your profile lines up with what we're looking for, we'll reach out and ask you to complete a 60-minute TestGorilla assessment for critical thinking skills, send us your resume, and maybe a couple of other items.

From there, we conduct between 2-4 video interviews. One of these might be a live technical assessment.

If the Culture Index step feels like a strange way to start a job application — that's kind of the point. Remember the phrase Think Different?

Ignition is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome and will consider all qualified applicants. Good luck in your search — and may the Force be with you!

#7658. Your Media Plan Might Be Missing Its Best Customers

If you plan media, you’re being asked to find new customers across more screens with fewer partners and to prove that what you’re doing worked. The IAB’s September outlook shows 63% of buyers say acquiring new customers is a top-three goal this year.

But the best media plan is only as good as the data behind it. The limiting factor is often not the sophistication of the targeting tools but what the underlying data can actually reveal. When advertisers rely on the same familiar signals, they risk overlooking valuable audiences that don’t fit their existing definitions.

That’s where carrier data can add a different perspective. By combining insights into mobile app activity with broader patterns of real-world movement, it can uncover connections between consumer behaviors that traditional audience strategies might miss.

Consider a pizza chain trying to acquire new customers. Its media plan might start with people who order from competing pizza restaurants, use pizza delivery apps or exhibit other signals of interest in pizza.

That’s a logical approach to winning market share. But it also assumes that the most valuable prospects are already interested in pizza.

In reality, consumers aren’t always choosing between pizza chains. They’re deciding what type of food they want in the first place. Reaching the right people and understanding what they’re deciding are two different problems.

What happens when you build an audience around that broader decision? Instead of limiting the search to pizza-related signals, marketers can incorporate observed behaviors across restaurant categories, mobile apps and real-world locations. That broader perspective can help identify consumers whose habits and interests make them promising prospects, even if they weren’t included in the original audience definition.

It’s a different way to approach the same marketing objective. Rather than simply refining a model to find more people who fit the presumed target audience, advertisers can use additional evidence to reconsider who belongs in that audience at all.

Advertisers are using T-Mobile carrier data to surface exactly these kinds of audience opportunities.

Take the users of one food delivery app. T-Mobile carrier data shows that this audience is 57% more likely than the national average to also use Gopuff. The audience overindexes on Grubhub and Uber Eats, too. That validates the competitive assumptions most plans start from.

But that same audience is also 45% more likely to be heavy streamers, and overindexes with fantasy sports fans, expectant parents and college students.

Together, these signals suggest an opportunity that a category-focused audience strategy might overlook, such as reaching people during a night in with a show queued up, a game on and dinner handed off to a food delivery app.

That doesn’t mean the data proves these activities are happening together. But it gives advertisers a new hypothesis to explore and potentially new audiences, messages and media placements to test.

A data set that only looks at one category can help find the next pizza order. But looking at data across apps and mobility patterns can reveal a broader range of behaviors and potential new occasions to reach consumers.

The effectiveness of audience modeling depends on the quality and breadth of the signals behind it. Carrier data provides a particularly useful foundation, combining observed app ownership and engagement with patterns of real-world movement and available demographic attributes.

Because consumers carry their phones throughout the day, these signals offer a perspective on behaviors that might otherwise be scattered across different apps, platforms and physical environments. Combining them at the audience level helps advertisers build a more complete understanding of consumer interests and activities without relying on individual-level tracking.

It’s also important to distinguish what’s observed from what’s modeled. Carrier data is observed and deterministic. The scale is modeled.

Platforms such as Blis and Vistar Media use carrier data as a starting point to model and activate audiences across connected TV, audio, mobile and digital out-of-home, including environments where traditional device identifiers aren’t available.

The modeling is only as good as what it starts from, which is why the breadth and quality of observed behavioral signals matter. And while identity still matters, strategies that don’t rely exclusively on any one identifier or platform provide additional resilience as advertising identifiers face continuing restrictions.

For media planners, four questions are worth exploring:

These questions expose a hard truth: A media plan can only be as comprehensive as the view of the consumer it’s built on.

Carrier data is a stronger starting point. Because it draws on observed behavior across apps and location patterns, it can inform more dynamic approaches to reaching customers. With Blis, carrier-informed audiences can be activated across omnichannel media. With Vistar Media, those same audiences can help identify relevant digital out-of-home screens by location, frequency and daypart. This approach can help brands strengthen existing connections and reach new audiences in relevant moments.

Tonight, people across the country will decide what to eat, with plenty of restaurants competing for their attention. Reaching them with a relevant message at the right moment requires more than knowing which restaurants they’ve visited or which apps they use. It requires understanding how their behaviors fit into a broader picture of their interests and habits.

The clearer that picture, the better equipped advertisers are to recognize valuable prospects, including the ones their original audience definitions overlooked.

#7654. Instagram is offering YouTubers up to $500,000 to post with its new horizontal format

Instagram isn’t just chasing YouTube‘s TV watch time and ad revenue–it’s chasing its talent, too. The Meta-owned platform has offered to pay some YouTubers up to $500,000 to post videos with its newly announced long-form horizontal format “Features.”

According to Business Insider, Instagram has approached “select” YouTubers with a floor price of $50,000; others have gotten six-figure offers, and things top out at a half-million dollars.

“We’ve been public about the fact that we are funding Features content directly with some creators right now to support them,” a Meta spokesperson told BI. “The details of those deals are confidential, but we’re excited to see the content going live.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

It’s not clear how Instagram is paying out these amounts–per video, per month, or as one-time flat compensation. We’d bet the latter, and perhaps the pot’s sweetened with a promise to pay creators performance bonuses or an ad rev share if their Features content does well (especially on TVs, where pricier ads slots can pull in serious cash for platforms).

Meta already said, though, that it’s “too early to share a long-term monetization model [for Features], but we’re exploring ways for creators to earn from brands, fans, and Instagram, including performance-based incentives.”

Introducing Features earlier this week, Instagram hyped its established TV viewership, with VP of Product Tessa Lyons saying “people love to watch Reels together in their living rooms with their friends, so we’ve been working on a TV version of Reels.”

“[W]e know to do that well, we need more than just short-form video,” she added.

Insta chief Adam Mosseri chimed in Oct. 28 after concern from creators, tweeting that “[w]e understand the economics matter a ton, and are exploring multiple options to help long-form creators get paid.”

This YouTuber-bait program is perhaps one of those options.

People familiar with the deals told BI Instagram’s terms just ask creators to post their long-form videos as Features on the same day they upload to YouTube.

Reza Izad, who reps Kareem Rahma, Noah Beck, and more as co-founder and co-CEO of Underscore Talent, told BI these deals are an “exciting opportunity” for YouTubers. The money is part of that excitement, sure, but Izad said this is also an opportunity for creators’ content to get a boost.

“Every time there’s a new feature in these apps that the company’s promoting, people will have more opportunity to be seen because there’s going to be algorithmic preference to this kind of content,” he said. “And unlike short-form, there’s not a lot of abundance.”

What he’s saying is true: We already know Instagram plans to pump posts made with Clips as Reels (a tool that takes snippets of Features videos and posts them to Reels with a link back to the full long-form upload) on its Explore page, and in other areas around the platform.

Something to think about in all of this is that a major part of YouTube’s living room success is the relative attractiveness and easy UX of its TV app. Google has put stock into making the TV app a banger, and Instagram isn’t there yet.

As Mosseri put it, “We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app, which […] is going to take some time to get it right. But I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long-term.”

Creators looking for equal viewership across YouTube and Features will likely be disappointed–at least for now. But for the folks Instagram wants to pay, this is indeed a rare chance to get get cash for cross-posting.

#7651. Smart Acquisition Or Frankenstack? Stagwell-Freestar And DoorDash-Instacart

It’s fall, and M&A is in the air. Two acquisitions happened this week: Stagwell bought Freestar, and DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart.

Here at AdExchanger, we’re always intrigued by the rationale for acquisitions – from the ones that feel like yin meeting yang to the ones that feel more like stitching together a Frankenstack. (Had to get a spooky reference in!)

In the first half of the podcast, we discuss Stagwell buying Freestar. Why would an indie agency want to build a company that helps open web publishers better set up their ad stacks? Our managing editor, Anthony Vargas, who covered the acquisition, talks about the hints the companies dropped, including how Freestar’s 1,000 publisher site connections could support Stagwell’s principal media business. Are we seeing a rehash of GroupM buying ad network 24/7 Real Media – 19 years later?

Then, when retailers merge, could the extremely fragmented retail media space defragment just a bit? At the time of the recording, DoorDash was in advanced talks to buy Instacart – and on Thursday, news dropped that the acquisition was official.

Pending approval, DoorDash Ads and Instacart’s Carrot Ads will likely come together. Carrot Ads also offers a white-labeled retail media business, which recently added Gopuff as a customer. So imagine Russian nesting dolls, or that image of a whale eating a shark eating a fish – because this type of M&A is going to change how marketers work with retail media companies, which our senior editor, James Hercher, discusses to close out this week.

#7650. This bike will stop your kid’s YouTube video if they’re not pedaling

Kids watch a lot of YouTube. And that generally means a lot of sedentary, butt-in-seat time.

But what if they had to pedal to keep the content coming?

That’s the question entrepreneur couple Arnav Dalmia and Shivani Jain are asking with their new company/product Tovie.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Described as a “sensory-friendly bike that helps kids use movement to self-regulate,” Tovie is a peddling machine where kids sit on whatever chair/couch/etc is comfortable and get their feet going. (If this sounds familiar: Yes, it’s basically like those under-desk peddlers for office workers. More on that later.)

The reason Tovie piqued our interest is Dalmia and Jain’s proprietary “Pedal-to-Play” system, which “makes movement the controller,” they say. It works by connecting Tovie to a kid’s device via Bluetooth, and whenever they stop pedaling, the YouTube video they’re watching (or the video game they’re playing) stops working.

The goal is to keep kids moving their bodies but still allowing them screen time.

“Studies done by researchers have found that movement in general is a tool for self-regulation of the hormones in their bodies, to help the nervous system calm down,” Dalmia told Inc. “It helps get the excess energy out before they have a big meltdown.”

He added that with Tovie, he and Jain feel they are “creating a whole new category of children’s fitness.”

“People think that children can get exercise while outside playing, but not all kids are the same, and they have different circumstances. In winter, it’s too cold outside. If parents are busy preparing dinner, they can’t watch their kids playing outside,” he added.

This isn’t Dalmia and Jain’s first stationary exercise product. In 2013, they debuted Cubii, an under-desk elliptical, and to bring it to life, they raised almost $300,000 on Kickstarter.

They’re producing Tovie the same way. This time, the Kickstarter goal is only $50K, and with nine days left in the campaign, they’re about to cross that threshold thanks to just over 100 backers.

Once they’ve shipped the initial models to Kickstarter supporters, the couple hope to put Tovie in big-box stores like Target and Walmart–and then keep developing products.

“The Tovie bike will be the first of many bikes focused on children’s health,” Dalmia told Inc. “Being a dad myself, I know how important physical movement is. The goal is to encourage movement and get kids started with fitness to start good lifelong habits.”

#7648. Down To The Wire To Acquire; Meta Wants To Be TV, Too

Are we in for a year-ending blockbuster M&A spree?

The Information jokes that CEOs ought to “get your deals in while ya still can, folks.”

A convergence of factors could make for a splashy Q4. As AdExchanger discussed in our Big Story Podcast last week, The Trump administration hasn’t been opposing acquisitions that would have drawn tough scrutiny under the Biden admin. Well, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu confirmed to The Information that he backed out of the company’s previous attempt to buy Instacart in 2021 because he worried Biden-era regulators would squash it.

Another factor in M&A’s favor: Many valuable businesses are struggling with risk-averse investors who don’t know how the AI revolution will shake out. The Information cites Duolingo, Coursera and Zoom as companies that have lost investor support but that would be attractive to buyers. They could join Bumble or Roku in limping to an exit.

Interestingly, what Duolingo, Coursera and Zoom have in common is that they’ve put little effort into earning ad revenue. In 2021, Zoom briefly tested a pilot ad program to monetize free users. That went away a year later.

These companies have the scaled user bases and first-party data assets marketers covet, but not much appetite for the ads biz. Could M&A flip the switch?

If YouTube’s TV, And Meta’s TV, Then Who’s Flying The Plane?

Everyone’s sick of the “Is YouTube TV?” debate. Great news: Now we can argue about whether Meta is TV, instead!

Last week, Meta announced that it’s testing long-form content on Instagram, allowing creators to share content up to 90 minutes long. The announcement comes alongside an influx of CTV spending among direct-to-consumer brands as platforms court midsize advertisers.

Cody Plofker, former CEO and CMO of makeup brand Jones Road, had been against TV advertising until he realized spending 80% of the company budget on Meta was limiting brand exposure, he said at Tatari’s Forward event in New York on Thursday.

Like Jones Road, many DTC brands have “[maxed] out social platforms” and are now putting more focus on TV advertising “as a performance vehicle,” Mike Shields writes in Next in Media.

And CTV ad platforms like Tatari are taking inspiration from Meta and Google by launching their own optimization engines.

Never one to back down from a fight, Meta is searching for its own spot in the TV landscape.

But YouTube is already known for engaged, loyal followings, Shields points out. And YouTube’s content is delivered on demand, which is a fit for TV, whereas Instagram’s algorithmic feed isn’t the traditional TV experience.

As one insider in the creator market tells Shields, why take away what’s working on YouTube TV and redirect resources to Instagram TV?

AI search is the new boogeyman robbing publishers of ad revenue. But another long-feared boogeyman – brand safety – can still spook the sell side.

Last week, former writers for the feminist news site Jezebel raised the alarm that hundreds of articles had been removed from the site. They pointed the finger at Jezebel’s new owner, Paste Magazine, which acquired the publication from G/O Media in 2023.

Anna Merlan, a former Jezebel writer now reporting for Mother Jones, says she heard from sources familiar with Paste that its publisher, William Sagan, decided to remove the articles after an “advertising and analytics company” flagged more than 4,000 articles as “not brand safe.”

But Sagan denied that Paste deleted the articles over brand safety concerns in statements provided to Mother Jones and The Washington Post. He says Paste often flags articles for any number of reasons, including grammatical errors, and temporarily reverts these stories to “draft” status. Indeed, many of the Jezebel articles taken down last week were republished soon after their authors started raising questions.

Paste’s exact motivation for taking the articles down remains unclear. But you can’t blame former Jezebel writers for being sensitive about brand safety.

Jezebel has long suffered monetization troubles tied to advertiser concerns over its coverage. Former Paste editor-in-chief Josh Jackson even claimed he never knew the extent to which brand safety solutions can demonetize publisher content until Paste acquired Jezebel.

#7644. AI Labels Don’t Tell Consumers Whether An Ad’s Claims Are Real

Disclosure: Sourin Chakrabarti works on AI labeling for advertising at Meta. The views expressed are his own and do not represent Meta.

In October 2025, three clips appearing to show police detaining and pepper-spraying protesters racked up millions of views across X, Instagram and TikTok. Created with OpenAI’s Sora, the videos carried visible watermarks, yet NewsGuard found that users still cited them as evidence that the events occurred. The footage crossed an unsettling threshold: It didn’t just look realistic; it functioned as visual proof.

Most concern about deepfakes has focused on politics. But the same tactic is now appearing in advertising, where synthetic content can make a product claim look proven.

In a recent campaign investigated by Full Fact, a supposed doctor claiming to be affiliated with Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust tested a weight-loss patch and appeared to grow thinner on camera. The trust called the posts “completely fraudulent,” while Google’s Gemini detected SynthID watermarks confirming AI involvement. Yet that watermark only revealed that AI was involved, not where the fiction ended. Was only the doctor’s face synthetic? Or were the medical authority, hospital connection, personal experience and physical transformation invented, too?

This exposes the fundamental blind spot of AI disclosures: they flag the production tool, not the illusion. A generic label tells consumers that AI was used to build an ad, but leaves them to guess where reality ends and fiction begins.

The fraudulent NHS weight-loss ad was not an isolated incident. In 2025, the Australian Medical Association warned that deepfakes impersonating prominent doctors were promoting unproven products, with clinicians discovering the fraud only when patients asked whether to swap prescribed treatments for advertised miracle cures. In 2026, Chinese regulators launched an enforcement campaign targeting businesses that mass-produced fabricated consumer-experience posts.

The legal principle predates generative AI. In FTC v. Colgate-Palmolive Co., a shaving cream commercial used a plexiglass prop in place of real sandpaper. Viewers were misled because the simulation was presented as a genuine product test. The case offers a useful test for AI advertising today: Does an ad merely illustrate a claim or does it ask viewers to treat a synthetic scene as real-world proof?

Platforms and regulators are building substantial disclosure systems to track synthetic content. Google displays “How this ad was made” panels, Meta attaches “AI info” labels and TikTok offers “AIGC” self-disclosure controls. Governments are pushing in the same direction: The European Union’s Article 50 rules require transparency for synthetic media, China mandates explicit AI markers and New York requires advertisements to identify synthetic performers.

Yet current AI-labeling systems mostly tell consumers that AI was used, not what it changed or why it matters. The same label can appear on an ad with a decorative AI background and one with an entirely fabricated testimonial. Those uses are not equally misleading, but a generic label may not distinguish between them.

Some policies address the clearest cases. The Advertising Standards Council of India’s 2026 draft guidance identifies fabricated experts, endorsements and exaggerated results as high-risk uses that labeling alone cannot fix. TikTok Shop prohibits AI-generated professional identities used to sell health products and alterations that misrepresent product performance. But a harder question remains: What about AI simulations that are lawful but could still be mistaken for real-world evidence?

The disclosure gap is becoming urgent as AI ad generation reaches industrial scale. In 2025, advertisers created three times as many Gemini-generated assets on Google as in 2024, including nearly 70 million in the final quarter alone. Meta has reportedly aimed to automate ad creation and targeting with AI by the end of 2026. Because these tools are embedded directly into ad-creation systems, safeguards cannot rely on post hoc consumer complaints. They must operate systematically across millions of ads.

The answer is not to label every synthetic pixel. Building on the IAB’s January 2026 disclosure framework, regulators should adopt a risk-based approach requiring specific disclosures whenever AI material appears to provide evidence for a product claim. This approach would produce three outcomes:

Platforms could implement this approach by requiring advertisers to disclose three things: the role played by any AI-created person or scene, whether the generated material depicts product performance or results and what real-world evidence supports the claim. Meta, Google and TikTok already accept advertiser declarations, so these questions could fit into existing workflows. Platforms should also retain a record of the advertiser’s answers and the notice shown to consumers, creating an auditable trail of how each ad was reviewed and presented. An emerging industry proposal calls this a served disclosure receipt.

Consider the weight-loss patch video. Under this system, an “AI was used” label would be only the starting point. The advertiser would have to identify the doctor as a synthetic expert, classify the apparent transformation as a product-performance claim and clarify whether the testimonial represented a real customer. It would also have to provide evidence supporting the weight-loss claim. If the doctor was falsely presented as real, the testimonial was fabricated or the result lacked substantiation, the ad would not be approved.

The goal is labels that answer the question consumers actually face: not just whether AI made the ad but whether AI made up the reason to buy.

#7639. Fox Doesn’t Want To Talk About Roku, But It’s Got Lots To Say About Tubi And Politics

Any investor hoping to ask about Fox’s pending Roku acquisition during its fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Monday was out of luck.

Fox’s IR rep made that clear up front and pointed analysts to Fox’s SEC filings instead.

However, CEO Lachlan Murdoch did share a mini update, including that shareholder and foreign regulatory approvals are in, although Fox is still working with the DOJ on antitrust clearance.

“[We] expect to close the transaction as soon as we can,” Murdoch told investors, noting that Fox’s “conviction in the opportunity has only grown.” Pairing Roku’s platform with Fox’s sports, news and entertainment content is a good recipe for building “our position in the fastest-growing segments of the media landscape,” he said.

Fox’s revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion in the quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue (60% in its TV segment) driven by the World Cup, early midterm spending and Tubi, its free ad-supported streaming service.

Tubi grew revenue 35% year over year, alongside a 23% uptick in total view time.

Fox attributed that engagement to a combo of Tubi’s content library, 10 new originals and a World Cup hub, which drew on Fox’s US English-language rights to the tournament.

Tubi also got a boost from viral content from more than 600 creators. Its Tubi for Creators program launched in 2025 with six creators and has since wooed big YouTube names like MrBeast and Jomboy Media.

And profits are growing, too, despite higher content costs, according to CFO Steve Tomsic, who noted that Tubi is contributing more to the bottom line than it was in the year-ago quarter when it turned its first profit – a development Murdoch himself apparently didn’t see coming.

A Bank of America analyst on the call reminded Murdoch that a year or so ago he’d said that Tubi’s growth, then in the midteens, wouldn’t be sustainable.

“I don’t remember saying that, but I’m sure I did … Thank you for calling me out on that one,” Murdoch said, adding that Tubi’s profit margins should settle in the 20% range once it reaches “further maturity.”

Advertising is the main engine behind Tubi’s momentum, which Murdoch said is continuing into the current quarter. Tubi’s audience is young, diverse and mostly cord-free, he said, which is like catnip for advertisers.

“They’re a very hard market for advertisers to reach,” he said, which, in a midterm year, is a pretty good pitch to political campaigns.

Fox booked more than $350 million in political ads this cycle, and Tubi was responsible for roughly $50 million of that.

Most of the rest – $250 million-plus – went to Fox’s local stations, including many in battleground states, where demand is so high that some stations run out of ad inventory. The remaining $50-ish million went to political ads across national sports, news and entertainment.

But if you squint, and not that hard, Tubi also kind of counts as local advertising in Murdoch’s view. “It’s effectively local revenue because it’s targeted,” he said.

Politics aside, sports has been a tailwind, too.

The FIFA World Cup final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history; the World Series, which aired on Fox, averaged 12 million viewers; and Fox’s NFL “America’s Game of the Week” is drawing an average of nearly 25 million viewers per game.

But Murdoch was also careful to temper expectations for Fox One, Fox’s streaming service for Fox content.

It’s not like there’s a World Cup every year – or a midterm election.

“It’s always a point in time,” Murdoch said. “Every couple years, you’ve got to be careful to understand the strength of the political cycle.”

And not everything at Fox was a win this past quarter, no matter how you spin it.

Fox News finished its fiscal Q1 as the most-watched cable news network, with 2.1 million primetime viewers and 1.3 million across all dayparts. But those figures were down 17% and 16% year over year, according to Nielsen, and Fox News was the only major cable news network to see declines. The slide has continued into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

Murdoch blamed tough comps against last year’s “tremendous news cycle,” which included the inauguration, Charlie Kirk’s assassination and DOGE-related drama. He compared this cycle to the 2006 midterms, when a second-term president was halfway through his term.

It’s not that viewers are defecting to CNN or MS Now, he said. They’re “just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall.” (Even so, Nielsen does show CNN and MS Now both up from last year.)

Meanwhile, cable advertising rose 8%, helped along by sports, but digital news ad revenue fell. Asked about that – we mourn you preemptively, open web – Murdoch pointed to Fox News Digital’s standing as the top news site in the US and called digital news a “hyper-competitive market.”

#7637. Affle Acquires Perion For $420 Million, Because ‘Synergies’

If you ask the executive leadership of Affle and Perion why the two companies are merging, the answer you’ll get is “synergies.”

Tal Jacobson, Perion’s CEO, is well aware that the term has become a total cliche. “Every time I write an email and use ‘synergy,’ Google pops up and says people don’t like that word,” he joked on Monday, the day after Affle agreed to acquire Perion for $420 million in cash.

But even so, it’s the best shorthand for what each company is missing that the other can supply, he told AdExchanger.

Affle is an India-based holding company for mobile ad tech built around performance marketing, largely in emerging markets, while Perion focuses on CTV, digital out-of-home and retail media. Most of its clients are big brands and agencies in developed markets, mainly in North America.

For the past few years, Perion has been evangelizing the concept of outcome-based advertising with its clients. But there was a hole in its offering. “We never had good performance-driven technology for mobile,” Jacobson said. “Affle has pure technology just for that.”

For its part, Affle gets a foothold with the agencies, holding companies and brands that Perion already works with, said Sameer Sondhi, Affle’s CEO of North America and chief strategic investments officer.

Perion, which has roughly 500 employees, will operate as a wholly owned subsidiary under Affle and brings the combined company’s headcount to just over 1,000 people. Jacobson, who will stay on as CEO, said that everyone from Perion is staying aboard.

LUMA Partners advised Affle on the deal, which is expected to close in early 2027.

AdExchanger spoke with Jacobson and Sondhi about how the pieces fit, what happens now to Perion’s own string of recent acquisitions and why Jacobson would rather call this a merger than a sale.

AdExchanger: Why sell to Affle and why now?

TAL JACOBSON: We don’t think about selling. We think about merging – taking two successful companies and making them a bigger engine of growth. “Selling” has a negative connotation, like somebody gave up, and that’s not the case.

Neither of us has the growth potential separately that we have together. We’ve spent a few good months working side by side, and the teams are working very well together.

Why is $420 million the right price? Perion paid $100 million alone to acquire Hivestack in 2023, $65 million for Greenbids last year and $12 million for PRN, which does in-store retail media, just a few months ago.

TJ: It’s a tricky question. For a public company, the right price is what investors will pay, and I don’t believe Perion was valued correctly in recent years. So, if the public market doesn’t see our long-term potential, why not join forces with someone who does?

The price doesn’t reflect the full long-term value; it reflects a point in time, and Affle wouldn’t buy this if it didn’t think the potential was bigger than the price.

SS: Both of us are listed, so the number is always going to be debated. There are plenty of public reference points – DoubleVerify, Nielsen, LiveRamp, IAS – and the boards have to approve. In the end, a number is a mindset thing.

Affle has been pushing a cost-per-converted-user (CPCU) model, where advertisers only pay for conversions. Will Perion’s DOOH, CTV and retail media inventory be sold that way?

TJ: Not necessarily. It depends on the channel and the customer’s goal. You can’t sell out-of-home on a CPC model, because you can’t click on an ad. But you can say, “Pay us for performance.”

Some formats might be CPC, others CPA or CPL. Whatever helps an advertiser’s business, that’s what we want to focus on.

So not CPCU, exactly, but a CPCU mindset?

TJ: We’re outcome-driven. The KPI is whatever defines success for that advertiser.

SS: With the targeting you can do on DOOH screens and the signals we get from mobile, the goal is to help clients with whatever way they’re used to buying. We don’t want to confuse them. We want to educate them.

Perion’s open web spend fell by around 23% in Q2. Doesn’t seem like a good sign for the future of the open web.

TJ: We’ve been telling investors and clients that the open web is not the future. Forget channels; focus on outcomes. When a CFO approves a budget, they don’t care if it’s websites or out-of-home.

And yes, everybody’s hyped about CTV, but if it doesn’t help the business, it doesn’t matter.

How much of this deal is about agentic AI?

TJ: Both companies have invested a lot in AI over the past two years. Our Outmax agent trades media, mostly in walled gardens, and Affle’s AI is focused on the deeper funnel and conversions. I don’t think we’ll merge the algorithms into one, but it helps to have all those tools under one roof.

SS: The systems don’t need to unify; they just need to talk to each other better.

Perion has made several acquisitions of its own and now it’s being acquired itself. How do all the nesting dolls fit together?

TJ: Affle lets every company it acquires stay independent under its own name and with its own road map and team. We’re not combining everything. Greenbids, for example, gives us the walled gardens – YouTube, Meta, TikTok – which neither Perion nor Affle had. PRN is just another extension of out-of-home, but inside retail stores.

The point is to sit in front of a CMO and be able to say, “Whatever you need, we probably have it.” We’ve worked hard over the past three years to roll up other companies, and this is just another phase of that.

This industry does not need 150 ad tech companies. It needs to consolidate.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.
